title: JavaScript — Comparisons, truthiness, and control flow

questions.question: How should you compare two values in new JavaScript?
options: Always == so that 0 and false count as equal.
=== which compares type and value with no conversion.
Python `is`.
A preprocessor #eq directive.
questions.explanation: === does not coerce. == does, and that is where the surprises live.

questions.question: An if block in JavaScript looks like which of these?
options: if score >= 90: then indented lines, Python-style.
if (score >= 90) { grade = "A"; }
if score >= 90 then grade := "A" fi
#if score >= 90
questions.explanation: Parentheses around the test, braces around the body. Same idea as C and C#.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: 0 == false is true. 0 === false is false. What should you use in new code?
options: === unless you have a specific reason to coerce.
== so that 0, "", and false all mean the same missing value.
Boolean(left) == Boolean(right) for every comparison.
!= only, because !== cannot compare numbers to booleans.
questions.explanation: == coerces. === compares type and value. 0 is a real amount, not false.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: This is called type coercion.

questions.question: What does console.log(null || "x", 0 || "x", 0 ?? "x") print?
options: x x x — all three operators treat 0 as missing.
x x 0 — || skips 0; ?? only substitutes null or undefined.
null x 0 — || keeps null and ?? keeps 0.
x 0 0 — || keeps 0 because 0 is a number.
questions.explanation: || uses truthiness, so 0 is replaced. ?? is nullish, so 0 stays.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: The || operator denotes logical or. It produces true if either of the values given to it is true.

questions.question: Which values are falsy?
questions.explanation: 0 and "" are falsy. "0" is a non-empty string. [] is a truthy object.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: if (amount) skips a zero-dollar payment. What is the better gate?
options: if (amount || amount === false) so that 0 is still skipped.
if (amount == false) because 0 equals false under ==.
if (amount != null && Number.isFinite(Number(amount))) including 0.
if (Boolean(amount) === true) which still drops 0.
questions.explanation: A missing amount and a zero amount are different. Test nullish and finite separately.

questions.question: customer.name || "guest" vs customer.name ?? "guest" when name is "".
options: Both yield "guest" because empty string is nullish.
|| yields "guest" and ?? keeps "" because empty string is not nullish.
|| keeps "" and ?? yields "guest".
Both throw because "" is not a valid string.
questions.explanation: ?? only replaces null or undefined. Empty string is a defined value.

questions.question: && and || in JavaScript return what?
options: Always a boolean true or false, like C++ && on bool.
Always 1 or 0 so they can be added.
One of the operands, which may be a string, number, or object.
A Promise, because they are asynchronous.
questions.explanation: "Ada" && customer returns customer. They short-circuit, but the result is an operand.

questions.question: Why is for...in a poor choice for walking payment rows in an array?
options: It freezes the array so push cannot run afterward.
It is the only loop that can see array length.
It skips index 0 the same way if (amount) skips 0.
It walks keys as strings and can include inherited names.
questions.explanation: Use for...of or a numeric index. for...in is for enumerable keys.

questions.question: C++ if (p) on a pointer means non-null. What is the JS trap for if (order.amount)?
options: 0, "", and NaN are falsy, so real data can look missing.
There is no trap; 0 is truthy in JavaScript.
Objects are always falsy until you call Boolean.
if cannot test numbers; you must use switch.
questions.explanation: JS if tests truthiness, not nullness. Amounts need an explicit numeric check.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: Which checkoutState result is correct for { status: "open", amount: 0 }?
options: missing, because 0 means there is no order.
zero, because a finite amount of 0 is its own state.
blocked, because 0 is not greater than 0.
ready, because status is open and any amount counts.
questions.explanation: The notes treat zero as a distinct payable state, not as missing or ready.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: [] is truthy. What does if (rows) hide when rows is an empty list of appointments?
options: JavaScript throws because arrays cannot be used as conditions.
The branch is skipped, so empty lists are handled automatically.
The branch still runs, so you must also check rows.length.
if (rows) converts the array to 0 because length is 0.
questions.explanation: Empty arrays are truthy objects. Check length when emptiness matters.

questions.question: value == null is sometimes used on purpose. What does it match?
options: Only null, not undefined.
Every falsy value including NaN.
null, undefined, 0, and false.
null and undefined, not 0 or "".
questions.explanation: That is the one common == idiom: a combined nullish check. It does not catch 0.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: There are two special values, written null and undefined, that are used to denote the absence of a meaningful value.

questions.question: Which loop is the default for walking an array of appointment objects?
options: for...of so you get each element value in order.
for...in so you get each object’s prototype keys too.
do...while, required whenever length might be zero.
while (true) with break on undefined, because arrays are infinite.
questions.explanation: for...of yields values. for...in yields keys. Empty arrays simply do not enter the body.

questions.question: const n = 0; console.log(n ? "yes" : "no"); prints what?
options: yes, because 0 is a valid number.
no, because 0 is falsy in the condition.
0, because the ternary returns the tested value.
undefined, because n is const.
questions.explanation: The ternary uses truthiness. 0 picks the else branch.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke

questions.question: isOpenStatus should accept only "open" and "pending". Which implementation is safest?
options: return status == true || status == "open".
return Boolean(status) && status !== "closed".
return status === "open" || status === "pending".
return status.includes("open") so "reopen" also passes.
questions.explanation: Strict equality to an allow-list. Loose checks treat unexpected strings as open.
